summary: This standards-track memo defines a minimal set of MIB objects for managing ISDN terminal interfaces with SNMP, using SMIv2.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard set of dials for checking on an ISDN phone-line connection.

questions: what objects does the isdn mib define
how does the isdn mib use ifstack
what is a spid in isdn
subtitle: A standard set of SNMP objects for watching and configuring ISDN lines, channels and signaling.

tldr.problem: Routers, terminal adapters and hosts with ISDN interfaces each reported their line, channel and call details in their own way, so network management tools had no common view of them.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines an SNMP MIB module, written in SMIv2, with five groups of objects for Basic Rate interfaces, B channels, D channel signaling and data link, terminal endpoints and directory numbers. Each channel is also represented as an interface in the Interfaces MIB and tied together with the ifStack table.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that works together with the Dial Control MIB (RFC 2128), which must also be implemented and which holds the peer and call history information.

today: RFC 2127 is a Proposed Standard published in March 1997, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be implemented together with the Dial Control MIB in RFC 2128.

sections.title: What the ISDN MIB Is
sections.content:
RFC 2127 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) used by network management protocols. It is a minimal set of managed objects for SNMP-based management of ISDN terminal interfaces. The RFC notes that ISDN interfaces appear on many kinds of equipment, including terminal adapters, bridges, hosts and routers, for both data and voice.

The module is written in a way that complies with the SNMPv2 SMI, and it fits the SNMPv2 framework: the SMI (RFC 1902), MIB-II (RFC 1213) and the protocol (RFC 1157 and/or RFC 1905). It was produced by the ISDN MIB working group of the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a rulebook that says how a device should report facts about its ISDN phone-line connection, so any management tool can read them.

sections.title: Five Groups of Objects
sections.content:
Managing an ISDN interface needs information about the physical interface, the B channels, the signaling channels, and optionally terminal endpoints and directory numbers. The memo splits this into five groups.

  • isdnMibBasicRateGroup: physical Basic Rate interfaces. For Primary Rate, the physical lines (T1 or E1) are managed in the DS1/E1 MIB instead.
  • isdnMibBearerGroup: B (bearer) channels, with configuration parameters and statistics.
  • isdnMibSignalingGroup: D (delta) channels, with three tables: isdnSignalingTable and isdnSignalingStatsTable for the Network Layer, and isdnLapdTable for the Data Link Layer (LAPD).
  • isdnMibEndpointGroup (optional): Terminal Endpoints, needed only for non-ISDN endpoints on a D channel or when Terminal Endpoint Identifier (TEI) or Service Profile Identifier (SPID) values are required.
  • isdnMibDirectoryGroup (optional): a list of directory numbers per signaling channel, needed only when accepted numbers differ from isdnSignalingCallingAddress.

Peer information and call history are deliberately left out. They live in the Dial Control MIB, so that part can also be used for non-ISDN interfaces such as modems or X.25 virtual connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The gauges are sorted into five drawers: the wire itself, the lanes that carry your data, the lane used for dialing, and two optional drawers for extra labels and phone numbers.

sections.title: Layering Onto the Interfaces MIB
sections.content:
An ISDN interface usually has one D channel and several B channels, all layered on a physical interface. The MIB models this by creating a logical interface entry (ifEntry) for each D channel entity and for each B channel, then relating them to each other and to the physical interface with the ifStack table of the Interfaces MIB.

Each D channel can support several Terminal Endpoints, which are either ISDN signaling channels or channels carrying X.25 based packet mode services. The ifType values are fixed by the memo, as shown below. The RFC gives an example in which a Basic Rate interface, a LAPD interface, an X.25 packet layer, two signaling channels, two B channels and two PPP peers each get their own ifIndex.

The ifTestTable and ifRcvAddressTable are not supported by this MIB. The memo also specifies, per interface kind, what each ifEntry column should return. For example, ifSpeed of a B channel is usually 56000 or 64000, LAPD speed is usually 16000 for basic rate or 64000 for primary rate, and ifMtu for LAPD and signaling is usually the Q.921 default of 260.
sections.plainLanguage: Every piece of the line, such as each lane or the dialing channel, gets its own numbered nameplate, and a stacking chart says which piece sits on top of which.

sections.title: Implementation Hints for ISDN Features
sections.content:
Section 3.4 of the RFC is a set of notes on how real ISDN features map onto the MIB.

  • Leased lines: set isdnBearerChannelType to leased(2); there is no signaling for them. With no signaling on a Basic Rate interface, isdnBasicRateSignalMode must be inactive(2).
  • Hyperchannels: a call that uses several B channels is counted as one call in isdnSignalingStatsTable, and the related isdnBearerTable entries hold identical values. Multiplexing can use the DS0Bundle MIB or several ifStack entries with the same HigherLayer; the implementor chooses.
  • D channel backup and NFAS: several LAPD interfaces can sit under one signaling entry, but only one is active; inactive ones have ifOperStatus of dormant(5).
  • SPIDs: defined for BRI only and used in North America. A switch can define up to 8 SPIDs per BRI. The SPID goes in isdnEndpointSpid, not in the calling address, because the two values can differ.
  • Speech and audio bearer capabilities: the network may treat Speech calls in its own way, so a modem is not guaranteed to work over them. Some users run 56 kbit/s data over Speech calls to use cheaper tariffs.
  • Incoming calls to router ports: a call can be matched by calling address, by called address (one isdnSignalingTable entry per router port), or by higher-layer means such as PPP authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: This part is a set of tips for odd cases, like a line that is rented all the time, or a call that uses several lanes at once, and how to write them down in the gauges.

sections.title: What an Implementation Must Support
sections.content:
The compliance statement makes three groups mandatory: isdnMibSignalingGroup, isdnMibBearerGroup and isdnMibNotificationsGroup. The Basic Rate group is mandatory for entities that support ISDN Basic Rate interfaces. The Endpoint and Directory groups are optional for all systems that attach to ISDN interfaces. The four Basic Rate objects may be implemented read-only.

The memo also says implementing the Dial Control MIB is required, while the DS1/E1 MIB is not required but recommended for Primary Rate entities. The DS0 MIB is optional.

The module defines one notification, isdnMibCallInformation. It is sent when an incoming call is rejected for policy reasons, when an outgoing call attempt ultimately fails (after all retries), and whenever a call connects. Only one such notification is sent between successful or unsuccessful attempts with a single neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: Some gauges are required on every device, some only if you have a certain kind of line, and a few are optional extras. One alarm bell rings when a call is turned away, fails or connects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of RFC 2127 is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. Anyone deploying the MIB has to look to the surrounding SNMP framework and to the Dial Control MIB (RFC 2128), which does discuss access to incoming calls.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not write down any safety rules in this document, so you have to find them elsewhere.
